title: India’s emerging quantum ecosystem strengthened by enabling policy of the Modi government: Dr Jitendra Singh
subtitle:
Supportive Ecosystem Is Giving India’s Quantum Startups the Confidence to Build, scale up and Compete Globally: Dr. Jitendra Singh

India Achieves 1,000-km Quantum Secure Communication in About Three Years Against 2,000-km Target Set for Eight-Year Mission, says Dr. Jitendra Singh

NQM Support to Quantum Startups Expands from 17 to 26; Government Building Infrastructure, Funding and Industry Linkages: Dr. Jitendra Singh

India Has the Potential to Become Globally Competitive in Quantum Communication and Sensing, Self-Reliant in Quantum Computing, Says Dr. Jitendra Singh

PRAGATI Q-FOUNDRY by Department of Science and Technology Brings Startups, Industry, Investors, Manufacturers and Strategic Users Together to Accelerate Quantum Technology Deployment

At PRAGATI Q-FOUNDRY 2026, Dr. Jitendra Singh Unveils 10 New Quantum Technologies, 9 Startups and Strategic Partnerships
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                30 SEP 2026 6:46PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India’s emerging quantum ecosystem is being strengthened by an enabling policy of the Modi government that is opening greater space for industry and the private sector to participate in frontier technologies, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, Dr. Jitendra Singh, said today. He said India had the scientific talent, technological capability and industry readiness, but the enabling environment provided by policymakers is now giving stakeholders the confidence to build and scale in quantum technologies.
Addressing PRAGATI Q-FOUNDRY 2026 – NQM Co-development and Venture Partnership Meet at Dr. Ambedkar International Centre, New Delhi, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the National Quantum Mission represents a new approach in which the Government, scientific institutions, startups, industry, investors, States and strategic users are working together to build indigenous capabilities. He said India would not remain a consumer of quantum technologies developed elsewhere and is building capabilities, infrastructure, talent and enterprises to develop these technologies at home and take them to the world.
The Minister highlighted the speed of progress under the National Quantum Mission, noting that the Mission was planned for eight years, but India has already achieved 1,000-km quantum secure communication in about three years, against the 2,000-km target envisaged for the eight-year period. He said achieving half of the target in less than half the planned timeframe demonstrates the capability that has been built within the quantum ecosystem and provides confidence to move ahead with greater speed and resolve.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the National Quantum Mission has been structured as a whole-of-government and whole-of-nation effort, with four thematic hubs at IISc Bengaluru, IIT Madras, IIT Bombay and IIT Delhi, bringing together 152 researchers from 43 institutions across 17 States and two Union Territories. The hubs are working across quantum computing, quantum communication, quantum sensing and metrology, and quantum materials and devices.
He said the progress achieved in the last two to three years shows that India now has an opportunity to become globally competitive in quantum communication and quantum sensing and self-reliant in quantum computing. The Minister said the technologies emerging from the hubs, academic institutions and startups are already providing a strong foundation for this ambition.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the Government’s support to startups is not limited to funding, but extends to infrastructure, mentorship, technology validation, industry partnerships and pathways to customers. He stressed that quantum startups require sustained engagement from industry and investors, including capital, technical validation, co-development, procurement and market access. He also called upon States to evaluate indigenous technologies developed by startups and explore their deployment and procurement so that promising ventures can become sustainable.
The Minister said early industry linkage is particularly important for the sustainability of quantum startups, as quantum technologies require substantial capital and long-term commitment. He said PRAGATI Q-FOUNDRY and the B2B interactions associated with it are intended to facilitate concrete outcomes such as technology validation, procurement, co-development, investment and partnerships rather than merely showcasing technologies.
The National Quantum Mission has already supported 17 startups, and nine additional startups were announced at the event, taking the total to 26. Dr. Jitendra Singh said the expansion reflects the Government’s continuing commitment to nurture quantum entrepreneurs and provide promising Indian ventures access to funding, infrastructure, mentorship and pathways to customers.
The event also witnessed the launch of flagship quantum technologies and products, exchange of MoUs and announcement of startups by Dr. Jitendra Singh. These initiatives mark the next phase of implementation under the National Quantum Mission, with the focus shifting towards testing, validation, integration, investment and deployment of indigenous technologies.
As part of the technology outcomes showcased under the Mission, one of the Technical Groups under the Quantum Communication Hub at IIT Madras successfully demonstrated a hybrid PQC-QKD link over 17 secure nodes between Chennai and Bengaluru using existing BSNL fibre. The 50ps daisy-chain timing synchronisation has also been released as an open-source solution for the research community.
The event was attended by Prof. Abhay Karandikar, Member, NITI Aayog; Prof. Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India; Prof. Umesh V. Waghmare, Secretary, Department of Science & Technology; Dr. J. B. V. Reddy, Mission Director, National Quantum Mission, along with senior scientists, entrepreneurs, investors, industry representatives and other stakeholders.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also interacted with founders of quantum startups in a roundtable discussion, taking stock of their technological progress, challenges and requirements for scaling. The interaction focused on strengthening linkages between startups, investors, industry and potential users so that promising indigenous technologies can move towards validation, adoption and deployment.
The Minister said indigenous capability in quantum processors, secure communication systems, advanced sensors, materials and devices is important for India’s technological self-reliance, particularly in critical and strategic domains. He said India must build domestic capability across the value chain while remaining globally connected and developing technologies that are internationally competitive.
Prof. Abhay Karandikar, Member, NITI Aayog, said the progress under the National Quantum Mission demonstrates the importance of bringing together government, academia, startups and industry to build a strong quantum ecosystem. He said the Mission is creating the foundations for indigenous technology development and greater participation of the private sector in this emerging field.
Principal Scientific Adviser Prof. Ajay Kumar Sood said the quantum ecosystem is demonstrating that the traditional linear model of taking 10–15 years to move from fundamental science to technology is changing. He said around 52 technologies at various Technology Readiness Levels have emerged from the four thematic hubs, along with 17 financially supported startups. He stressed that deployment and procurement of indigenous technologies will be critical for making startups sustainable and creating internationally competitive products.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the success of PRAGATI Q-FOUNDRY should ultimately be measured by the technologies advanced, partnerships created, investments mobilised, startups strengthened and indigenous solutions taken into use. He called upon all stakeholders to move forward with clear commitments, timelines and responsibilities, and said the National Quantum Mission has laid the foundation for India to build globally relevant quantum technologies and national capability.

title: Scientists map earliest glow of hydrogen, opening a new window to the universe
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                30 SEP 2026 5:17PM by PIB Delhi
content:
In an international collaboration that includes researchers from India, the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment telescope (CHIME telescope) has made its first standalone detection of the glow of hydrogen from when the universe was about five billion years old, paving the way for new studies of cosmic expansion and dark energy.
The CHIME interferometric radio telescope in Canada was built to map the distribution of hydrogen gas in the early universe, allowing astronomers to calculate its expansion and thus investigate dark energy, the mysterious force thought to be driving the universe to expand faster over time.
In a study that included CHIME collaborators at the Raman Research Institute (RRI), an autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST), the CHIME telescope has shown, for the first time, that it can detect the faint glow of hydrogen gas from deep in the universe's past using only its own data.
The breakthrough paves the way for a faster, less expensive method for scientists to study dark energy — the mysterious force thought to be driving the universe to expand at an ever-increasing rate, and one of the biggest open questions in physics. The achievement also marks a milestone for the telescope, built for this very reason. The findings are published in a paper today in The Astrophysical Journal.
Fig
: A view of CHIME at night, with the Milky Way in the background Credit_ CHIME collaboration
“Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe and the raw material from which stars form,” said co-author Dr. Arnab Chakraborty, postdoctoral fellow at the University of Toronto who first proposed the finding. “Its faint radio emission acts like a cosmic tracer, revealing how matter is distributed across space.”
There are contradicting theories about the nature of dark energy in the astrophysical community. Using its own data, CHIME can investigate these theories independently and help prove or disprove them.
“This is a completely new technique for probing the cosmos, delivered by an instrument that was conceived, built and funded by Canadians,” said co-author Dr. Mark Halpern, professor in the University of British Columbia and CHIME principal investigator.
“CHIME is a unique instrument that scans a large fraction of the cosmos as the sky drifts over it. With no moving parts and high accuracy measurements, CHIME delivers a snapshot of what our sky looks at radio wavelengths everyday!”, added co-author Dr. Saurabh Singh, associate professor at RRI.
Previously, CHIME had to cross-correlate its observations with galaxy survey data from other telescopes. Galaxy surveys investigate the same question, using light and focusing in fine detail. They cost millions more dollars, and they focus just on the part of the universe hot and dense enough to form stars.
By mapping the combined radio glow that hydrogen emits on its own, CHIME can explore the same questions at a greater scale, further back in time, at a fraction of the cost and without relying on anyone else’s results.
In an accompanying paper, the researchers examined what the observed signal reveals about the distribution of hydrogen in the universe.
“Our data indicate that roughly two per cent of the hydrogen in the universe was in neutral atomic form at this time, broadly consistent with other measurements” said co-author Dr. Shabbir Shaikh, postdoctoral fellow at Arizona State University. “By measuring how that hydrogen is distributed and clustered, CHIME gives us a new way to test our understanding of how galaxies form and evolve”.
The finding wasn’t a Eureka moment. The research applied new data analysis and processing techniques to find the faint signal amongst the overwhelming noise of the background universe, human technology and even the instrument itself. They then spent more than a year testing the finding to prove it was correct: it was indeed a call from the universe itself when it was about five billion years old, based on 94 nights of observation data collected in 2019.
The current measurement uses only a small fraction of the data CHIME has collected since operations began. Researchers now have nearly seven years of observations available and are working to expand the analysis to include earlier periods in cosmic history when the universe was only three billion years old.

content:
As part of the
Swachhata Hi Seva (SHS) 2026 Campaign
, themed
Swachhata Mein Sahbhag, Swachh Bharat, Viksit Bharat,
the Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment organized the national level
SafaiMitra Suraksha Evam Samman Shivir
in the National Capital here today.
The theme of the Shivir was
Samman Safai Mitron Ka, Sankalp Swachh Bharat Ka.
The national-level programme was organised in hybrid mode, in which Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), Rural Local Bodies (RLBs) and line departments participated virtually from across the country.
The programme was attended by Smt. Rekha Gupta, Hon’ble Chief Minister, NCT of Delhi; Dr. Virendra Kumar, Hon’ble Union Minister for Social Justice & Empowerment; Shri B. L. Verma, Hon’ble Minister of State for Social Justice & Empowerment; Shri Pravesh Wahi, Mayor, Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD); Shri Sanjeev Khirwar, Commissioner, MCD; Dr Sandeep R. Rathod, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment; Shri Prabhat Kumar Singh, Managing Director, National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC) along with senior officers of the Ministry and officials of MCD, among other dignitaries.
The
Shivir
at Kedarnath Sahni Auditorium, Dr. S.P.M. Civic Centre, was organized to recognize and honour the contribution of SafaiMitras and sanitation workers and facilitate their access to healthcare, safety, welfare and social protection measures. It provided a single-window platform for sanitation workers and their families to obtain information and assistance regarding various Government schemes and services, while reinforcing the importance of their contribution to public health, cleanliness and the well-being of communities.
Addressing the gathering, Smt. Rekha Gupta, Hon’ble Chief Minister, NCT of Delhi, emphasised that sanitation workers are being provided appropriate safety equipment and that their contribution must be recognised with dignity and respect. She highlighted various initiatives of the Delhi Government for different sections of society, including the Pink Card facility providing free bus travel to women, the Lakhpati Bitiya Yojana, 450 Arogya Mandirs for multiple health tests and 611 Palna Kendras for the children of working women.
Smt. Rekha Gupta stressed that maintaining cleanliness is not the sole responsibility of SafaiMitras and sanitation workers but a collective responsibility of every citizen. She called for ensuring that sanitation workers receive their rightful entitlements and emphasised that the safety and dignity of women sanitation workers deserve particular attention. She also highlighted measures to promote mechanisation of sanitation work, including the recent approval of 1,000 litter-picking machines and 100 sweeping machines, aimed at reducing risks associated with manual cleaning activities. She further informed that a top-up health coverage of ₹5 lakh over the existing ₹5 lakh Ayushman Bharat coverage would enhance the total health coverage available to beneficiaries to ₹10 lakh.
Dr. Virendra Kumar, Hon’ble Union Minister for Social Justice & Empowerment, highlighted the Government’s efforts under the NAMASTE Scheme to extend support and welfare measures to Sewer and Septic Tank Workers and Waste Pickers. He emphasised that ensuring the safety and dignity of sanitation workers remains a key priority and that sustained efforts are required to facilitate their integration into the mainstream of society.
Dr. Virendra Kumar underlined that NAMASTE goes beyond welfare assistance by focusing on the safety, dignity and long-term social and economic inclusion of sanitation workers. He highlighted the extension of benefits to Sewer and Septic Tank Workers and Waste Pickers and stressed the importance of ensuring that eligible workers are connected with healthcare, social security and safety-related interventions. He emphasised that sanitation workers should be enabled to lead lives with dignity and become an integral part of the mainstream of society.
Shri B. L. Verma, Hon’ble Minister of State for Social Justice & Empowerment, highlighted the Government’s sustained focus on sanitation and the welfare of sanitation workers since 2014. He noted that the scope of the NAMASTE Scheme has been extended to workers associated with Fecal Sludge Treatment Plants (FSTPs) and Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs), along with benefits such as Ayushman Cards and PPE kits.
Shri B. L. Verma emphasised that access to welfare benefits must be accompanied by adherence to prescribed safety guidelines and protocols. He also underlined the importance of citizen participation and responsible behaviour towards sanitation workers, reiterating that cleanliness and the dignity of persons engaged in sanitation work are a shared responsibility.
Shri Pravesh Wahi, Mayor, MCD, highlighted the importance of safeguarding the rights and welfare of sanitation workers. He informed that more than 3,000 SafaiMitras had been formalised in the MCD and emphasised the provision of appropriate safety equipment, including PPE kits, to enable sanitation workers to perform their duties safely.
Shri Sanjeev Khirwar, Commissioner, MCD, acknowledged the efforts of the Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment and MCD towards strengthening sanitation work and improving support for sanitation workers. He also appreciated the contribution of NSKFDC in facilitating welfare and support measures for sanitation workers.
The Shivir also provided an opportunity for sanitation workers and their dependents to access a range of health, safety and social protection services. Preventive health check-ups and screening services were facilitated for SafaiMitras and their dependents, while PPE kits and other safety equipment were distributed and demonstrated. Eligible sanitation workers and their families were facilitated in accessing Central and State Government welfare and social protection schemes. The programme provided information and facilitation relating to schemes and services such as Ayushman Bharat/PM-JAY, PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana, Swachhata Udyami Yojana and PM Jan Dhan Yojana, subject to eligibility. Assistance was also provided regarding eligibility criteria, application procedures and registration processes for various welfare and social protection schemes.
Parallel programmes were also organised by Urban Local Bodies across the country. These programmes featured live webcasting of the national-level event and included activities aimed at promoting the dignity, safety, health and welfare of sanitation workers. Eligible SafaiMitras, sanitation workers and waste pickers were facilitated in accessing relevant benefits and services, including PPE kits, Ayushman Cards and other welfare and social protection measures.
The gathering also took the Swachhata Pledge, reaffirming a collective commitment towards cleanliness, hygiene and responsible civic participation. The pledge reinforced the spirit of
“Swachhata Mein Sahbhag”
and encouraged citizens to contribute towards creating a cleaner and healthier India.
Besides, the
Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan
pledge was also administered in which the gathering participated reaffirming their commitment to
Drug Free Society-Drug Free India.
A film on
NAMASTE
Scheme was screened on the occasion.
On the occasion, the Ayushman Cards with upto Rs 5 Lakh healthcare coverage, were distributed among the SafaiMitras.
The SafaiMitra Suraksha Evam Samman Shivir reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to placing the health, safety, dignity and social security of sanitation workers at the centre of the Swachhata Hi Seva campaign. The programme highlighted the vital contribution of SafaiMitras and sanitation workers to public health, cleanliness and the quality of life of communities across the country.
On this occasion, the experts demonstrated the safety drill while sporting PPE kits and other safety gear.
The nationwide observance provided an opportunity to recognize and appreciate SafaiMitras and sanitation workers for their essential contribution and to strengthen collective efforts towards ensuring their safety, dignity, welfare and social security. It reinforced the message that the vision of a Swachh Bharat and Viksit Bharat can be achieved through the active participation, protection and recognition of every individual contributing to sanitation and cleanliness.

content:
Timely counselling, rehabilitation and behavioural support can play an important role in helping individuals overcome harmful influences, rebuild their confidence and return to productive livelihoods. Targeted support can also help beneficiaries regain focus, strengthen family financial stability and move towards a more disciplined and self-reliant life.
At 23, Prakash Londhe (name changed), a Scheduled Caste beneficiary from Nagpur, Maharashtra, was struggling with the negative influence of a peer group.
The situation affected his routine and distracted him from his auto-rickshaw business, resulting in irregular working hours, missed peak-hour commuters, poor daily earnings and financial instability. His family was deeply concerned about his future and the economic difficulties caused by his inconsistent income.
Seeking to break free from harmful habits and regain focus on his livelihood, Shri Londhe received support under the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR) at Navjeevan Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addict, Nagpur, an Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA). The intervention provided professional psychological counselling, motivational sessions, behavioural support, rehabilitation assistance and peer-refusal training to help him resist negative influences.
Through counselling and behavioural support, Shri Prakash developed greater awareness of the harmful effects of bad company and substance abuse. With continued guidance and emotional support from his family, he successfully cut ties with the negative peer group and adopted a more disciplined routine. He is now focused on operating his auto-rickshaw business regularly and making better use of peak-hour demand.
By working full-time and targeting peak rush hours, Prakash Londhe has seen a significant improvement in his daily rides and income. The improvement has helped stabilise his family’s financial condition and strengthened his confidence in pursuing his livelihood.
Prakash Londhe’s journey demonstrates how counselling, rehabilitation and family support can help an individual overcome negative influences, regain focus and move towards greater economic self-reliance. His experience reflects the importance of timely support under NAPDDR in enabling beneficiaries to rebuild their lives with discipline, dignity and renewed purpose.

A brief note about the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) 2024-25
Coverage of ASI:
The Annual Survey of Industries broadly covers the following
Factories registered under Sections 2m(i) and 2m(ii) of the Factories Act,1948
Bidi and cigar manufacturing establishments registered under the Bidi & Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act,1966
Electricity undertakings engaged in generation, transmission and distribution of electricity, not registered with the Central Electricity Authority (CEA)
Units with 100 or more employees registered in the Business Register of Establishments (BRE) prepared and maintained by the State Governments as and when such lists are shared by the respective State Governments.
ASI frame and its updation
The ASI frame is based on the lists of registered factory / units maintained by the Chief Inspector of Factories (CIF) in each State and those maintained by registration authorities in respect of Bidi and Cigar establishments and electricity undertakings. The frame is being revised and updated periodically by the Regional Offices of the Field Operations Division of NSO in consultation with the Chief Inspector of Factories in the State. At the time of revision, the names of the de-registered factories are removed from the ASI frame and those of the newly registered factories are added. For the units selected in the last survey year (in this case 2023-24), relevant fields like Status Code, Frame industry (NIC 4 digit), Employee (Total persons engaged), Address etc. of frame for a given year, say, ASI 2024-25 are auto-updated dynamically based on the information collected during the last survey year.
Unit of Enumeration
The primary unit of enumeration in the survey is a factory in the case of manufacturing industries, a workshop in the case of repair services, an undertaking or a licensee in the case of electricity, gas & water supply undertakings and an establishment in the case of bidi & cigar industries. The owner of two or more establishments located in the same State and pertaining to the same industry group and belonging to census scheme is, however, permitted to furnish a single consolidated return. Such consolidated returns are common feature in the case of bidi and cigar establishments, electricity and certain public sector undertakings.
Data Collection Mechanism
Data for ASI are collected from the selected factories under the Collection of Statistics Act 2008 as amended in 2017 and Rules framed there under in 2011. The entire survey is conducted through a dedicated web-portal without any paper schedule. For data collection in ASI, an establishment (and not enterprise) approach is followed wherein data are collected from the selected establishments.
Survey Disclaimer
Various quality checks are carried out on the data collected through this survey which is primarily record- based. Relative Standard Errors (RSE) (which is a widely accepted statistical measure of reliability of an estimate) for important parameters estimated from the survey at an overall level are small and well within the acceptable range. However, since the data presented in this result are estimated from sample survey, necessary caution may be taken while using this data.

, at the existing rates and under the prevailing guidelines.
Operational since
7 March 2019
, the Scheme provides remission of eligible embedded State and Central taxes and levies that are not refunded through other mechanisms. Anchored in the principle of
zero-rating of exports
, it seeks to ensure that such domestic tax incidences do not burden exported products, thereby strengthening the global competitiveness of India’s apparel and made-ups sector.
During
2025–26
, the Scheme benefited more than
15,400 exporters across over 444 districts
, with the beneficiary base comprising
predominantly MSMEs
. Its wide geographical reach underscores the Scheme’s role in supporting a dispersed manufacturing ecosystem and strengthening the participation of small and medium exporters in global markets.
The extension will ensure
policy continuity and predictability for exporters
, while sustaining the competitiveness of India’s labour-intensive and value-added apparel and made-ups sector in an increasingly competitive global trading environment.

title: Bankers Books Evidence Act, 2026
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                30 SEP 2026 5:41PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 modernises India’s legal system governing admissibility of banking records as evidence. It comes into force on October 1 2026, and replaces the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891. The Act introduces a technology-neutral framework covering physical, electronic and digital records, with standardised provisions for their authentication and certification. It strengthens procedural safeguards governing the production of bankers’ books. The Act also protects bank officials from routine appearance in proceedings, where the bank is not a party, solely for the purpose of proving/testifying the record of the bank. It enables extension of its provision to specified financial sector entities, supporting an evolving and increasingly digital financial ecosystem.
A Modern Legal Framework for Banking Records
The Government has undertaken reforms to strengthen India’s banking and financial sector and improve ease of doing business. These efforts also focus on modernising laws and regulations to reflect the changing needs of the economy.
The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 comes into force on October 1, 2026,
and replaces the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891.
The Act provides clear and updated rules for admissibility of bank records as evidence in legal proceedings. It applies to court cases, inquiries, arbitrations and investigations where banking records may be required to be produced as evidence.
Breaking Down Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026
The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026
provides a
modern framework for admissibility of banking records as evidence
in line with contemporary digital banking practices. The Act will be
used in any legal proceeding
, an arbitration and any investigation or inquiry under the
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023,
or under any other law for the time being in force, in which evidence is or may be taken. As per the Act-
“Bank” and “banker”
mean any company or corporation carrying on the business of banking, any entity or class of entities operating in the financial sector (to whose books the provisions of this Act are extended), any post office savings bank or money order office.
“Bankers’ books”
include ledgers, day-books, cash-books, account books and all other records used in the ordinary course of business of the bank. These can be kept in written or physical form or stored in any form of data storage mechanisms
Need for the Act
The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act was framed in the colonial era of 1891, when banking systems were entirely paper-based. In the current times, India continues to progress in digitising its economy.
Banking and financial transactions are largely driven by digital platforms,
frequently accessible with a simple click on a mobile phone. In such a scenario, it is imperative that India’s legal framework evolves to keep pace with these advancements.
Key Features
The Act establishes a
contemporary evidentiary framework for banking records
, covering records maintained across physical and digital banking systems.
It enables
standardised authentication and certification of bankers’ books
, providing for appropriate certification of physical and electronic records.
The Act strengthens
clarity and procedural safeguards in the production of bankers’ books
. It also
protects bank officials
from being routinely required to produce records or testify in proceedings where the bank is not a party.
It provides a
flexible framework for extending the law across the financial sector
, as it continues to evolve in India.
The Act provides for stringent and contemporary safeguards for the secure handling and verification of electronic records as a precondition for their admissibility as evidence in legal proceedings.
Major Changes under the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026
The 2026 Act
retains the core evidentiary framework of the 1891 law for proving banking records through certified copies of records
. It modernises and strengthens the existing framework with a
technology-neutral system
covering electronic and digital banking records.
Recognition of Electronic Records as Evidence:
As per the new Act,
an electronic or digital record of a banker’s book will be admissible, valid, and legally enforceable as evidence
, subject to a few conditions which include-
(i)
the said copy is a true copy of such entry or information, and correctly represents or is appropriately derived from such records
(ii) no unauthorised changes to data are detected
(iii) no tampering or other event affecting the integrity and accuracy of the system is detected
This change standardises the certification process and allows authentication through manual, digital, and electronic signatures.
Compelling Production of Bankers’ Books:
The Act provides that the contents of a banker’s book may be proved in legal proceedings through a certified copy, without requiring production of the original banker’s book.
Accordingly, a bank officer cannot ordinarily be compelled to produce the banker’s book or appear as a witness to prove the records, particularly where the bank is not a party to the proceedings.
The Act provides that a bank officer may, however, be required to appear as a witness or produce a banker’s book only pursuant to a written order of the Court recording
a special cause.
The Act specifies the circumstances constituting a special cause, where-
(i) accuracy or authenticity of the entry or information is uncertain.
(ii) the regularity or ordinary nature of record keeping is interrupted owing to any event.
(iii) the bank does not comply with any previous Court order about inspection or production of the certified copy of the books.
Extension to Other Financial Sector Entities:
The 1891 Act applies to entities engaged in the business of banking and any post office savings bank or money order office. The 2026 Act also retains this clause.
However, it further allows the Government to
extend its provisions to any entity or class of entities operating in the financial sector
, by notification. The Government may highlight conditions, exceptions, or modifications in the notification.
Conclusion
The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 marks a significant step towards modernising the legal framework governing banking records. By
aligning evidentiary provisions with technological advancements and evolving economic needs
, it strengthens the efficiency, reliability, and adaptability of India’s financial system. It reflects the Government’s continued commitment to advancing reforms that strengthen institutions and support India’s growth trajectory.

title: Beyond Cleanliness: The Women and Transgender Changemakers of Swachhata
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                30 SEP 2026 1:18PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A clean city is often noticed through what is no longer visible. Waste no longer lies on the street. Drains no longer remain clogged. Sanitation facilities are available when they are needed. But behind this visible change are journeys that deserve to be seen too. They are the
journeys of women
creating livelihoods from waste, leading cleanliness efforts in their communities and turning everyday challenges into opportunities. Alongside them are
transgender community
members finding professional roles and recognition in sanitation services. Across cities, Swachhata is becoming more than a public service. It is becoming a space for
dignity, enterprise, participation and opportunity.
This spirit of participation finds a national platform in
Swachhata Hi Seva 2026,
launched on 17 September 2026. Every year, the campaign brings
citizens, institutions and leadership
together to strengthen
voluntarism and collective action
for
Swachhata.
With the theme
“Swachhata Mein Sahbhag; Swachh Bharat, Viksit Bharat”,
Swachhata Hi Seva 2026
places shared responsibility at the heart of the cleanliness movement. It underlines that the vision of a
Swachh and Viksit Bharat
calls for a
Whole-of-Government and Whole-of-Society approach.
Such a collective spirit finds a meaningful expression in Loni, Uttar Pradesh, where something once treated as waste is becoming a source of livelihood.
When Waste Becomes a Livelihood
Around gaushalas and dairies, cow dung can become a difficult waste-management challenge, clogging drains and sewage channels. In Krishna Vihar Colony of Loni, however, a group of women saw a different way forward.
They began using cow dung to make incense sticks and Loban cups.
What started with just 8-10 women grew into a livelihood opportunity for many more. A woman officer of the Loni Nagar Palika Parishad saw the potential in their work and helped connect the producers with gaushala owners for steady supply and utilization of cow dung.
A simple idea began to take root: what if something treated as waste could be given another life?
During the summer months when incense production is at its peak, the initiative employs
around 40-50 women
. For these women, the work is more than making a product. It brings together
livelihood, dignity, and the satisfaction of turning waste into something useful
. The Nagar Palika Parishad also earns
up to 25 per cent revenue
from the sale of these products. This creates a link between waste management, local enterprise, and municipal revenue.
The products themselves carry the story of reuse. Traditionally, making incense products requires wood sawdust as the base material. Mixing around 30-35 per cent dry cow dung powder reduces the quantity of wood sawdust required. This has emerged as an environmentally sustainable solution that also ensures swachchta
What began in one colony has travelled much farther. The products are supplied to several parts of the country, including
Delhi, Mumbai, Punjab, Gujarat and Hyderabad.
During the COVID period, they were also produced for major brands, with orders reaching
Mauritius and South Africa.
And the women are not stopping there. Plans are being explored to make
combustible wood as fuel from cow dung
for use in cremation grounds, havans, and other activities. The initiative is also exploring
cow-dung flower pots
that can eventually return to the soil as manure.
Here, the idea of cleanliness extends beyond removing waste. It means asking what else that waste can become.
From Waste Collectors to Waste Leaders
A similar spirit can be seen in Patna, Bihar, where women are
breaking old conventions and giving cleanliness a new, inclusive face
. At the city’s
Pink Material Recovery Facility (MRF),
women stand at the heart of the
waste-management process
. Operated primarily by women and led by a female supervisor, the facility
processes dry and wet waste
. It can manage
2 tonnes of dry waste and 1.5 tonnes of wet waste every day
.
The idea for the Pink MRF emerged from an effort to create
opportunities for women in the waste-management sector
. The project team approached the
Patna Municipal Corporation (PMC)
with the idea of establishing a Pink MRF. PMC supported the idea, and the facility was set up in
just three months
. Its distinctive colour and design also drew the attention of local people, helping create awareness around the initiative.
The idea reaches the community through the
‘Cash for Waste’
initiative. Citizens can bring dry waste and receive payment at prescribed rates.
Waste gains value, citizens gain an incentive to participate, and the city gains another set of hands in its cleanliness journey.
Patna’s Swachhta journey then takes an interesting turn. Old, unusable vehicles have been
given a second life as mobile Pink Toilets
. What once stood as scrap now serves a vital sanitation need. It is the spirit of the 3Rs:
Reduce, Reuse and Recycle
, made visible on the streets
.
Together, the Pink MRF and mobile Pink Toilets reflect
social justice, environmental awareness and economic opportunity
. Above all, they carry a simple message:
when women are given space in Swachhta, they do not merely become part of the system. They help reshape it.
Women Who Carry Cleanliness into Their Communities
The story of women and Swachhta does not end with the waste they handle.
It grows through the communities they touch.
In Bhopal, a
group of 250 women brand ambassadors
has worked with the municipal corporation on cleanliness and waste management. The group members have also established
‘Bartan Banks’
across 25 wards to eliminate the use of single-use plastic. By providing reusable utensil sets for community functions and events, these banks ensure that local gatherings are organized under zero-waste principles.
The
60-member ‘Swachhata Kitty Group’
has found another way to turn togetherness into action. Each woman
contributes ₹
100 every month,
creating a shared pool for community cleanliness activities.
Small contributions, carried by many hands, become a collective commitment to a cleaner neighbourhood.
In Uttarakhand, this spirit has taken the name
‘Bainni Sena ’-the ‘Army of Sisters’.
Across 57 groups,
570 women monitor cleanliness activities
in their wards. They interact with citizens, help communicate complaints, conduct awareness programmes, and support coordination between the municipal administration and sanitation workers. Their work happens where a city’s cleanliness is truly decided. It takes shape
in neighbourhoods, in conversations and in the small moments when someone chooses to care.
In Shillong, the
Iynnehskhem Self-Help Group
has found a new path to livelihood through waste. The women collect wet waste from homes and
turn biodegradable waste into compost
. Once involved in waste picking, they received training through a rehabilitation initiative and built a new livelihood around composting. Their unity earned them the affectionate name
‘Meri Maidens of Marton’.
Through their everyday efforts, the women are turning Swachhta from a responsibility into a shared culture of care.
When Inclusion Changes the Face of Sanitation
In Odisha
, transgender persons
are taking on roles that place them at the heart of urban sanitation systems. The change began in Cuttack, where the Municipal Corporation organised transgender persons into a Self-Help Group. They were trained and entrusted with the
operation and maintenance of a Septage Treatment Plant
.
It was a significant shift. A community that has often faced exclusion from formal opportunities was now taking responsibility for a technical sanitation facility.
The model subsequently expanded across Odisha.
Urban Local Bodies began partnering with Self-Help Groups
in Faecal Sludge and Septage Management (FSSM) and solid waste management.
In Bhubaneswar, the
Swikruti Self-Help Group
took responsibility for operating and maintaining a 75-KLD Faecal Sludge Treatment Plant (FSTP) at Basuaghai. Members received orientation and technical and managerial training before taking up their responsibilities.
For Meghna Sahoo, President of Swikruti, the transformation is deeply personal.
“Now, we can proudly embrace our identity and participate in the professional space,”
she says. She speaks of the pride she feels when members of her group explain their work to students and visitors from national and international institutions.
The significance lies not only in the job itself, but in what the job makes possible: professional identity, confidence and recognition.
The Bhubaneswar Municipal Corporation has also brought transgender groups into the operation and maintenance of seven cesspool vehicles. Drivers and helpers are to be engaged with minimum applicable wages. They will also receive training on health, hygiene, personal protective equipment, and desludging protocols. Odisha's pioneering move to expand livelihood options to transgenders has won many accolades. It has set the ball rolling for others to follow, showing how inclusive participation can pave the way for better sanitation.
The Deeper Meaning of Swachhata
These stories show that Swachhata can do more than create cleaner surroundings. It can open doors to livelihoods, participation, and recognition
. The real transformation lies not only in what happens to waste, but in what becomes possible for the people who manage it.
When people once pushed to the margins find a place at the heart of
Swachhata,
cleanliness takes on a deeper meaning.
It becomes a shared effort, shaped by dignity, opportunity and a sense of belonging.

title: Beyond Wastewater: Turning Used Water into a Resource
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                30 SEP 2026 12:26PM by PIB Delhi
content:
In growing cities, the water cycle does not end when water is used. What flows away from homes, businesses and neighbourhoods does not have to become waste. With the right systems, used water can be collected, treated, recycled and returned to productive use. This shift is shaping a new approach to urban sanitation under the
Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban (SBM-U)
. At its heart is
Used Water Management (UWM)
, which focuses on treating used water, preventing untreated sewage from reaching water bodies, and enabling safe reuse. Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) are central to this process, turning wastewater management into an opportunity to protect natural resources and recover water for further use.
This approach is reinforced through the
Water Plus certification
, which provides cities with guidelines for managing wastewater generated by households and commercial establishments. It requires wastewater to meet satisfactory treatment standards before being discharged into the environment. The focus extends beyond treatment infrastructure to how cities plan and manage their water resources.
Urban Local Bodies
are being empowered to formulate long-term, city-level plans for wastewater reuse. Clearly defined responsibilities and technological advancements are helping cities improve the efficiency and effectiveness of treatment systems. The
Open Defecation Free (ODF) ++ protocols
further strengthen this approach by assessing the safe management and treatment of entire sewage, including faecal sludge and septage.
Together, these measures are laying the foundation for sustainable sanitation and a circular economy, where used water can be managed as a resource. Under SBM 2.0, projects worth
₹11,785 crore
have been approved for setting up sewage treatment plants in small cities. These projects will add
4,900 million litres per day (MLD)
of treatment capacity, expanding the infrastructure needed for effective used water management.
Where Used Water Finds a Second Life
The management of used water is evolving beyond conventional treatment and disposal. Different cities are developing approaches that match their infrastructure, water needs and local conditions. In the process, treated water is finding applications in agriculture, horticulture, industry, road cleaning and lake rejuvenation. The experiences of cities like Jaipur, Indore, Surat and Navi Mumbai highlight some of these varied approaches.
Jaipur: Engineering Water Reuse at Scale
Water Treatment at Dehlawas Plant
Built over
22.50 hectares during 2020–23, the
Dehlawas Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) in Jaipur
has the highest sewage treatment capacity in Rajasthan, at
215 MLD
. Wastewater is effectively treated and converted into a reusable resource, thereby promoting the concepts of circular economy and water conservation. This high-technology plant is fully automated through a
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA)
system.
The plant discharging treated water into the Dravyavati River
Jaipur STP is currently equipped with a highly efficient
Sequencing Batch Reactor (SBR)
. In this process, wastewater passes through a Parshall flume, primary clarifier and basin before reaching the chlorine tank. It is then converted into clean water. Solid waste is separated using primary sludge thickeners and screw press machines. Once treated at the STP, wastewater becomes a valuable resource once again. It is being reused for irrigation and various industrial processes, a practice known as
wastewater recycling
, which is also an economically viable option. At present, a portion of the treated water is being supplied to a nearby colony
for gardening and other purposes. The remaining clean water is discharged into the
Dravyavati River
, while measures are being taken to ensure that untreated wastewater does not enter the river. A green area has also been developed around the plant, with
more than 30,000 plants
adding to the greenery of the site.
Indore: Leading the Water Plus Journey
Indore’s transformation in used water management began with a simple goal: keep untreated wastewater out of the environment. This approach helped the city become the first to receive Water+ Certification. Its practices demonstrated how sustainable sanitation and used water management could work at the city level. The model has also encouraged several smaller cities to pursue similar approaches.
Today, no untreated wastewater flows through Indore’s rivers or its natural and man-made stormwater drains. By 2020, the city had
7 decentralised STPs
alongside
3 existing centralised STPs
. It had also laid more than
200 kilometres
of piped network for carrying treated wastewater. Indore simultaneously strengthened measures for conserving both groundwater and surface water. In 2022, more than
1.25 lakh
rainwater harvesting units were installed across residential and non-residential areas. The installations were completed within a span of just four months. Treated wastewater is now used for water gardens, roadside plantations and horticulture. It is also used for washing roads and cleaning sewer machines.
Surat: Making Wastewater an Economic Resource
Water Treatment Plants in Surat
Surat has taken the idea of wastewater reuse further by treating it as a resource with economic value. The Surat Municipal Corporation has established four tertiary treatment plants with a combined installed capacity of
116 MLD
. The plants have helped reduce dependence on freshwater resources. Treated wastewater is reused across several non-potable applications in the city. These include industrial use, lake rejuvenation, agriculture, mass plantation, sewer cleaning, etc., through direct service lines and tanker filling stations. The city has
170 sewer-cleaning machines
, including equipment based on
Latest Advanced Robotic Technology
. These machines are used for cleaning and maintaining the sewerage system.
Navi Mumbai: Reuse Built into City Services
Sewage Treatment in Navi Mumbai
Navi Mumbai’s Water+ journey has combined treatment infrastructure with extensive reuse of treated water. It is the only city in Maharashtra to achieve a
five-star rating
and Water+ Certification. The city upgraded its sewage treatment technology and designed its STPs for a population of 30 lakh. Its pumping stations were also upgraded to reduce energy costs. These stations transfer sewage generated to the STPs. Preventive maintenance of the sewer network was undertaken to avoid hotspots. Navi Mumbai has achieved
100% mechanised cleaning
of sewer lines and septic tanks. Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation centrally monitors all septic tanks through Level Transmitters installed across the city. More than
30%
of treated water is reused in over 30 city gardens. It is also used to wash solid-waste vehicles, compactors and city transport buses. Sprinklers and road dividers also use treated water, reducing dependence on freshwater.
Tirupati: A Revenue Model for Treated Water
Tirupati
has developed a self-sustaining model for operating a sewage treatment plant at Thukivakam. The city has also been declared Water Plus. Built at a cost of
₹19 crore
, the STP has an installed capacity of
50 MLD
. It serves
1,04,057 households
across the city. Of the treated water,
24 MLD is reused
for various purposes. The plant sells
5 MLD
of treated used water to
Srikalahasthi Pipes Ltd.
With this, the plant is able to generate a net revenue of Rs. 6 Lakhs per month. Another
18 MLD
of treated used water is supplied free of cost to farmers for agriculture. The ULB also reuses a portion for road and street cleaning. Treated water is further used for watering road medians, parks and gardens across the city. These measures help maximise the reuse of treated water. Tirupati’s approach combines wastewater reuse with a revenue-generating model for sustainable STP operations.
Water Treatment Plant in Tirupati
A Shift in the Urban Water Story
The growing focus on used water management is changing how cities approach their water needs. Treatment is no longer only about preventing pollution. It is also about recovering water for productive use. Treated water is finding new uses in irrigation, industry, horticulture and everyday urban services. As more cities strengthen treatment capacity and develop reuse systems, urban water management is becoming more circular and resource-efficient. This shift helps build cleaner sanitation systems while making better use of every available water resource.
Reference
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

title: UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
subtitle: A Century of Meritocracy and Inclusion
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                30 SEP 2026 11:34AM by PIB Delhi
content:
On 1 October 2026, the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) completes one hundred years. Its institutional journey began on 1 October 1926, when India’s first Public Service Commission was constituted - an advisory body whose Chairman and Members were appointed by the Secretary of State in London. Over the century that followed, the Commission evolved in structure, status and responsibilities, becoming what it is today - an independent constitutional body.
The Road to 1926
The principle that entry into public service should rest on merit rather than patronage took formal shape in
1855
, when the Indian Civil Service (ICS) examination was instituted in London, replacing the East India Company’s system of nomination with open competition. For most Indians, however, the door remained nearly impossible to open. The examination was held only in London, in English, and tested candidates on subjects such as Greek and Latin - not because these were needed to govern a district in Bengal or Punjab, but because they favoured those educated in the British system.
In
1862
, 21-year-old
Satyendranath Tagore
, elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore, sailed from Calcutta to England to sit an examination his own country would not let him take at home. He cleared it in 1863 and joined the service in 1864 - the first Indian in what the British called the “heaven-born service”. He served for over thirty years in the Bombay Presidency. Six years after his success, Surendranath Banerjee, Behari Lal Gupta and Romesh Chunder Dutt followed. The maximum age for the examination was, however, progressively reduced from 23 to 19, leaving Indian candidates little time to prepare. By 1919, only
78 of the 1,255
ICS officers were Indian.
Sustained nationalist demands brought gradual change. The
Government of India Act, 1919
, enacted after the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, provided for a Public Service Commission. In
1922
, the ICS examination was held in India for the first time, at Allahabad, alongside London. In 1928 the Indian centre moved to Delhi. In
1924
, the
Lee Commission,
chaired by
Arthur Hamilton Lee,
recommended the immediate establishment of a statutory Public Service Commission. It also proposed that of every ten new entrants, four would be British, four Indian and two Indians promoted from the provincial services - on paper a path to parity, in practice a guaranteed 40 per cent of every intake for the British, by birth rather than by competition.
The Commission was established under the Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1926, framed under Sections 96B and 96C of the 1919 Act. Sir Ross Barker, a member of the Home Civil Service of the United Kingdom, was its first Chairman, assisted by four Members, and the Commission was housed at
Metcalfe House, Delhi
. Its limited powers drew sustained criticism from leaders of the freedom movement. Yet a permanent recruiting body now existed in India, seated and staffed in India - which is why the Commission dates its history from 1926.
The Constitutional Mandate
On
22 August 1949
, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee, moved the draft articles on the Union and State Public Service Commissions in the Constituent Assembly. They became
Part XIV (Articles 315–323)
of the Constitution. In his valedictory address on 26 November 1949, Dr. Rajendra Prasad emphasised that the independence of the Public Service Commissions was essential to ensure impartiality in public appointments and to guard against jobbery, nepotism and favouritism.
Article
What it provides
315
Public Service Commissions for the Union and for the States, with provision for a Joint Commission for two or more States
316
Chairman and Members appointed by the President
317
Removal or suspension of a Member only by order of the President, after an inquiry by the Supreme Court
318
Power to make regulations on the conditions of service of Members and staff
319
Restrictions on holding office after ceasing to be a Member; the Chairman is ineligible for further employment under the Government of India or a State
320
Functions: conducting examinations for appointment to the services of the Union, and advising on methods of recruitment, promotions and disciplinary matters
321
Power of Parliament or a State Legislature to extend the Commission’s functions
322
Expenses of the Commission charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
323
Annual report to the President; cases where the Commission’s advice was not accepted, with reasons, laid before Parliament
What the Commission does
Recruitment by examination:
The Civil Services, Indian Forest Service, Engineering Services, Combined Medical Services, National Defence Academy & Naval Academy, Combined Defence Services and Central Armed Police Forces (Assistant Commandants) examinations, among others.
Recruitment by selection:
Interviews and recruitment tests for specialist posts requisitioned by Ministries and Departments.
Advice to Government:
On Recruitment Rules, promotions through Departmental Promotion Committees, induction into the All India Services and disciplinary cases. In 2023-24, it processed the records of 24,581 officers for promotion, and 532 officers were inducted into the All India Services.
Police leadership:

Anecdotes
Short stories from the Commission’s century.
Where the ‘steel frame’ speech was made
Metcalfe House, built in 1835 by Sir Thomas Metcalfe, has a second claim to history. On 21 April 1947, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel addressed the first batch of civil service probationers there and described the civil services as the “steel frame of India”. The date is now observed every year as Civil Services Day.
A Maharaja’s transit house
Dholpur House on Shahjahan Road was built in 1920 in the Art Deco style by Maharaja Rana Udaybhanu Singh of Dholpur, as his residence during visits to Delhi. After Dholpur State merged with the Union on 7 April 1949, the building became government property. Three years later, in 1952, it became the Commission’s permanent headquarters.
One among eighty
In 1972, Kiran Bedi became the first woman selected by the Commission for the Indian Police Service, a service that had never had a woman officer. Of the eighty vacancies that year, she was the only woman.
Forms in the newspaper
In 1989, when slow post made it difficult for application forms to reach remote areas, the Commission printed them directly in newspapers. In 1984, when heavy snowfall cut off Kangra, it extended the application deadline by two weeks for affected aspirants.
A sun on a stamp
On 8 November 1977, the Posts and Telegraphs Department issued a 25-paise stamp for the Commission’s Golden Jubilee. It showed the sun - symbolising impartiality and equal opportunity for all - with the national tricolour. For the Platinum Jubilee, inaugurated by Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee on 14 December 2001, the Department of Posts issued a First Day Cover.
DID YOU KNOW?
The UPSC Museum, opened on 11 November 2016, is free and open to the public on weekdays from 9:30 am to 6:30 pm; a 360-degree virtual tour is available on the Commission’s website.
The age limit has travelled a long way. As late as 1988, an expert committee recommended keeping the Civil Services Examination age band at 21 to 26 years. The limits of 32 years for General candidates, 35 for OBC and 37 for SC and ST candidates, with up to ten years more for Persons with Disabilities, were fixed in 2014, when two extra attempts were also allowed.
Candidates who had appeared in the Civil Services Examination 2011 were given one more attempt in CSE 2015, whatever their age or the number of attempts already used.
The Commission has not always recruited only for the Union. In 1960-61, under Article 320, it agreed to recruit for bodies such as the Delhi Municipal Corporation, the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation and the Territorial Councils of the Union Territories.
Open competition lapsed during the Second World War. The London examination was held for the last time in 1939, officers for 1940, 1941 and 1942 were nominated directly, and recruitment through the British Civil Service Commission stopped altogether after 1943.
In the draft Constitution, the provisions on Public Service Commissions were numbered Articles 284 and 285 when Dr. B.R. Ambedkar moved them in the Constituent Assembly.
Case Studies: How the Machinery Works
Every morning in Mumbai, around 5,000 dabbawalas collect nearly two lakh home-cooked lunches and deliver each to the right desk by lunchtime, using nothing more than a colour code chalked on the lid. The Commission solves a comparable problem every year, at far higher stakes: the right question paper must reach the right candidate at the right minute, and every answer must then be judged on merit alone. The following case studies explain how.
Case Study 1:  The right paper to the right candidate
A candidate makes only one choice: the city. Within that city, the system allots the venue and the room, so that by the day of the examination every candidate has a unique address - city, venue, room, candidate - known in advance only to the system. Candidates in the same room may be writing different papers - in the Civil Services Main Examination alone, candidates choose from 48 optional subjects - so each sealed packet must carry exactly the papers needed at that venue, sorted room by room.
Case Study 2:  Setting a paper no one has seen
Question papers are built from question banks prepared by academic experts who work in anonymity under a strict code of confidentiality. No single expert sets a whole paper, and no expert knows which questions will be used, or when. In constructing a paper, the Commission ensures that it covers the entire syllabus, that its difficulty is balanced, and that no question has been asked in any previous UPSC examination.
The whole apparatus rests on the principle of ‘need to know’: no single person - not even the Chairman - sees the full picture.
Case Study 3:  Securing the examination hall
In collaboration with the National e-Governance Division, the Commission piloted
AI-enabled facial authentication
- matching a candidate’s live image with the application photograph - at select centres in Gurugram during the NDA & NA (II) and CDS (II) Examinations on 14 September 2025. It was implemented at scale at the Civil Services (Preliminary) Examination on 24 May 2026, where face authentication was carried out for all of about 5.50 lakh candidates through invigilators’ mobile phones, taking about 6–8 seconds per candidate.
Ahead of the CS (Preliminary) Examination 2026, a scan of fifteen years of candidate data identified and rejected
569 applicants
who had furnished false information to claim extra attempts.
Case Study 4:  Recruiting at the speed of need
The Commission has repeatedly scaled up when the nation required it, without lowering its standards. In July 1948, a Special Recruitment Board recruited experienced personnel aged 27 to 45 into the IAS and IPS on the basis of records and interviews. In 1956–57, a special drive screened over 22,000 candidates. In 1958, a Special Recruitment Board selected 197 scientists and technologists - including applicants from overseas - for a national Pool whose strength rose to 500 by 1962. During the 1962 emergency, an Emergency Commission filled 1,353 defence-related posts in two months.
During COVID-19, with train services disrupted, the Commission reimbursed airfare to interview candidates as a one-time measure, requested States to let candidates with e-summon letters move through restricted zones, helped with lodging and transport, and handed each candidate a sealed kit of mask, face shield, sanitiser and gloves.
Case Study 5:  Inclusion by design
Access comes first.
The Commission introduced scribes for visually impaired candidates in 1994, and today the right to a scribe and extra time is an entitlement for Persons with Benchmark Disabilities, who are also allotted the centre of their choice, may bring an escort, and are assisted by a facilitator at interviews. Women candidates receive fee exemptions. Age relaxations have been extended to those whose preparation was disrupted by events beyond their control - freedom fighters of the Goa liberation (1961–62), Indians displaced by the Bangladesh Liberation War and the Uganda-Zanzibar crisis (1971–72), and Indians affected by the Gulf War (1991).
Fairness follows:
an evaluation system, from written papers to the interview board, that is blind to identity. The Commission did not write the policy of reservation, but it built the national platform that implements it, including the Economically Weaker Sections category from CSE 2019 and a separate transgender category in its Online Recruitment Application form from 2020.
Case Study 6:  Merit beyond the merit list: Pratibha Setu
Candidates who clear every stage of an examination but narrowly miss the final list are not lost to public service. Under the Public Disclosure Scheme, in force since 20 August 2018 and first used for the Combined Medical Services Examination, 2017, the details of such willing candidates were made available to employers. Revamped and renamed
Pratibha Setu
on 9 June 2025, it connects them with verified employers, including Ministries, PSUs, autonomous bodies and private organisations.

title: Scientific Steering Committee on One Health Reviews Progress Towards Strengthening One Health Systems in India
ministry: Office of Principal Scientific Advisor to GoI
date:

                30 SEP 2026 7:19PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Sixth Meeting of the Scientific Steering Committee on One Health was held on 30 September 2026 at Kartavya Bhavan 3, New Delhi under the chairmanship of Prof. Ajay K. Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India.
At the outset, substantial progress made in operationalising the One Health approach beyond its initial convergence framework was noted. Prof. Sood underscored the importance of clear institutional ownership, outcome‑oriented targets, and consistent follow-through to ensure that the Committee’s recommendations translate into action on the ground. He also highlighted the value of building on ongoing programmes, established platforms, and current institutional capacities rather than creating parallel structures. Prof. Sood noted that such alignment would improve information flow, support coordinated decision‑making, and enable timely action across human, animal, and environmental health domains.
The Minimum Standard Requirements (MSR) document for BSL-3/4 laboratories developed by the Advisory and Review Committee on BSL 3/4 laboratories was released during the meeting. The document will shortly be made available in the public domain for wider dissemination and reference.
The Committee reviewed progress towards developing an interoperable One Health Dashboard and deliberated on areas requiring continued inter-sectoral coordination. The Committee also appreciated efforts made by MoH&FW towards the next phase of the Integrated Health Information Platform
(
IHIP) and noted that there are potential complementarities between IHIP and the proposed One Health Dashboard. Members discussed opportunities to strengthen existing systems and mechanisms and advance the implementation of One Health priorities at the national and sub-national levels.
In his concluding remarks, Prof. Sood commended the progress made in developing an interoperable One Health Dashboard. He urged Ministries and Departments to sustain collaborative engagement, strengthen follow‑up processes, and identify areas where greater convergence and support could accelerate implementation. He emphasised that an interoperable One Health Dashboard reflects not only a whole‑of‑government effort but a whole‑of‑country approach providing integrated visibility across sectors and ensuring that health threats are addressed holistically rather than in isolation.
The meeting reaffirmed the Government of India’s commitment to advancing an integrated One Health approach and strengthening national preparedness through coordinated, cross‑sectoral action.
The meeting was attended by Dr Parvinder Maini, Scientific Secretary, Office of PSA (OPSA) and secretaries of stakeholder ministries/department which included Dr Rajiv Bahl, Secretary, Department of Health (DHR) and Director General (DG) Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR); Prof Umesh Waghmare, Secretary, Department of Science and Technology (DST); Dr Mangi Lal Jat, Secretary, Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE) and Director General (DG), Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR); Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary, Ministry of Ayush; Dr V. Narayana, Chairman, Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO); and Dr Srinivasa Kumar Tummala, Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES). Participants also included Dr Rakesh Gupta, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoH&FW); Dr Naveena B. Maheswarappa, Animal Husbandry Commissioner, Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying (DAHD) and other Senior representatives from ICMR; Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change (MoEF&CC); Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) & Security Services; DAHD; ICAR; Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Ayush; National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC); Department of Fisheries; National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), National Institute for One Health (NIOH); OPSA and Gujarat state representatives. Additionally, the meeting was joined by the chairs of the Advisory and Review Committees viz. Lt. Gen. (Rtd.) Dr Madhuri Kanitkar (BSL-3/4 laboratory network), Dr N.K. Arora (technology-enabled surveillance), and Dr Vijay Chandru (data integration and data sharing) and members of Technical Working Group for One Health Dashboard.

In order to encourage discovery, development and commercialisation of new medicines and to support Start-ups and MSMEs, the Department of Pharmaceuticals, has announced a
New Discovery track
under
the Promotion of Research and Innovation in Pharma & MedTech (PRIP) Scheme for undertaking Pharma Innovation projects.
The objective is to encourage and enable start-ups and MSMEs to venture in to high-risk innovation ecosystem for discovery of new drugs and therapies.
This new track seeks to address a critical funding gap in early-stage novel drug discovery. Financial assistance of upto
₹50 crore per company/project/portfolio of projects will be provided, subject to a minimum co-funding of 25% of the project cost(s) from bona fide institutional investors.
This will act as large-scale risk capital to startups/ MSMEs and catalyse participation of institutional investors at an earlier stage of drug development, enabling more indigenous New Chemical Entities and New Biological Entities assets to progress from discovery towards clinical development and help build a globally competitive drug innovation pipeline.
Start-ups and MSMEs undertaking NCE/NBE projects at Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) 1, 2 or 3 are eligible to apply under this new exclusive track. The Department would support such projects to progress to higher TRLs not beyond TRL 6. The online PRIP portal is now open for submission of applications under the
second call of the scheme.
With a financial outlay of
₹5,000 crore
, the Scheme aims to strengthen India’s
pharmaceutical and MedTech research and development ecosystem
by supporting startups, MSMEs and large companies to move up the innovation value chain.

New Medicines

maximum of 35%
